title: Repairing a hole in crochet fabric
subtitle: Replacing damaged stitches by working a patch from the existing surrounding fabric
excerpt: A hole in crochet fabric is usually the result of a broken yarn or a snagged stitch. The repair involves unpicking back to the nearest intact round or row, reworking the missing stitches, and weaving in the new ends. Unlike woven fabric, crochet can be repaired in a way that is nearly invisible if the same yarn is available.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing). Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: A repair method in which individual stitches are replaced by threading a needle with matching yarn and retracing the path of each damaged stitch on the surface of the fabric, without unpicking the surrounding rows.
In crochet, a run occurs when a stitch breaks and the yarn unravels upward through the chain of stitches above it, creating a ladder-like gap in the fabric.

content.text: Repairing a hole in crochet fabric means replacing the missing stitches rather than darning over the gap the way you would on woven cloth. Crochet stitches lock into each other in a chain; once a stitch breaks, those above and below it remain intact. You remove the broken section, work replacement stitches into the surrounding loops, and weave in the new ends.

The result is nearly invisible if the repair uses the same yarn from the same dye lot. A different dye lot shows; a different yarn weight is visible. Start by identifying a spare length of matching yarn before beginning the repair.

items.name: Matching yarn from the same dye lot if possible
items.note: Save a small amount from the original project for repairs.

items.name: Crochet hook, matched to the yarn
Stitch markers
items.note: To mark the intact stitches at the edges of the damaged area before starting

content.text: Small damage (one to four broken stitches): the most common scenario. The stitches below and above are intact. Work replacement stitches directly into the existing loops.

(a ladder of broken stitches running up through several rows): the broken stitch propagated upward. Each damaged row needs to be addressed individually, working from the bottom of the ladder to the top.
Secure any loose ends at the edges of the hole by threading them onto the tapestry needle and weaving them back through the surrounding stitches. Do not cut them yet.
Cut a fresh length of repair yarn. Join it to the loop at the left edge of the hole (or right edge, depending on the direction of the original fabric).

Work replacement stitches of the same type as the original fabric across the gap. Insert the hook into the intact loop at the lower edge of the hole and work upward, matching the stitch count and height of the surrounding fabric.
Fasten off and weave in all ends, including the original loose ends from the hole, over a length of at least 5 cm going in two directions.

is an alternative for thin or abraded fabric where individual stitch strands have worn through but the structure of the row is still mostly intact. Thread the tapestry needle with a fine matching yarn and retrace the path of each worn stitch, passing the needle under the same loops the original yarn passed through. This reinforces the surface without removing any stitches.

items.symptom: The repair is visible as a patch in a different texture
items.cause: The repair yarn is from a different dye lot, or the repair stitches were worked at a different tension from the original fabric.
items.fix: Work the repair at a slightly looser tension to compensate for the fact that the surrounding fabric has stretched with wear. The repair stitches are new and will initially be tighter than old ones.

items.symptom: The fabric around the hole is unravelling further as you work the repair
items.cause: A broken stitch has begun a run that is continuing upward as you work.
items.fix: Stop the run immediately: insert the hook into each loose loop as you reach it and work a slip stitch to lock it in place. Then work the full repair from the lowest broken stitch upward.

items.symptom: The repair ends are working loose after a few uses
items.cause: The ends were woven in over too short a distance.
items.fix: Weave in ends over at least 5 cm, going in two different directions. In slippery yarn (silk, bamboo, smooth cotton), go a full 8 to 10 cm and split the yarn at the end to increase grip.

content.text: Practice on a test swatch first. Work a small square, cut one stitch, pull the yarn to open a hole, then repair it. This run-through shows you each step before you work on something that matters.
